title: Coercive Control, the Invisible Basis of Abuse
summary: Josh and Chuck explore coercive control, a pattern of non-physical and physical domination within intimate relationships that underlies much domestic abuse. They trace its roots to Albert Biderman's 1950s study of coercion tactics used on Korean War POWs, then to 1970s feminist work on battered women, Evan Stark's coining and development of the term, and Leonora Walker's battered women's syndrome. They cover the Francine Hughes "Burning Bed" case, legal defenses like temporary insanity, the debate over whether coercive control is gender-specific or can be mutual, and legal responses such as UK criminalization and California's civil approach. The episode includes a trigger warning, a hotline mention, and a listener mail recommendation of the documentary The World Before Your Feet.

segments.title: Opening and trigger warning
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode with a trigger warning, distinguish domestic violence from intimate partner violence, and preview coercive control as the underlying basis of much abuse.

segments.title: Biderman's coercion tactics and the Korean War POWs
segments.summary: Albert Biderman studied how Korean War POWs were coerced into collaborating, rejecting the brainwashing explanation and listing tactics such as threat, isolation, humiliation, exhaustion, occasional indulgences, and trivial rules. Feminist scholars in the 1970s later noticed parallels with how battered women were treated.

segments.title: Battered women and the Burning Bed case
segments.summary: The hosts describe 1970s and 1980s attitudes toward wife battering as a private matter and the 1984 TV movie The Burning Bed, based on Francine Hughes's abuse by Mickey Hughes over a thirteen-year period.

segments.title: Temporary insanity, battered women's syndrome, and learned helplessness
segments.summary: Francine Hughes was charged with first-degree murder and acquitted using temporary insanity after public support. Psychologist Leonora Walker developed battered women's syndrome and the concept of learned helplessness, which critics say excludes women who do not fit a submissive victim profile, such as Black women.

segments.title: Anne Flitcraft, Evan Stark, and coining coercive control
segments.summary: Anne Flitcraft found that many women in the ER had been beaten by partners, and her work with Evan Stark led him to identify coercive control as the foundation of much domestic abuse. Stark's 2007 book formalized it, and he testified for abused mothers in New York to keep their children. The hosts discuss how controlling behaviors such as criticism and dinner rules were normalized.

segments.title: Signs of coercive control: isolation, finances, surveillance, humiliation, threats
segments.summary: The hosts list coercive control tactics including isolation, financial restriction, monitoring, control of daily life and sex, humiliation, and threats. Michael Johnson's term intimate terrorism is introduced alongside situational couple violence and violent resistance. Separation often intensifies control.

segments.title: Is coercive control gender specific or mutual?
segments.summary: Researchers including Evan Stark and Kristin Anderson argue coercive control is largely male dominance of women, while a 2022 UK study found women perpetrators more often use it than physical abuse. An Australian 2021 study found higher-earning women faced increased risk. The hosts discuss whether mutual abuse is a myth, and note same-sex couples can also experience it.
topics: earning more and domestic violence risk

segments.title: Legal responses: criminalization, California civil law, and risks
segments.summary: The UK criminalized coercive control while California made it a civil violation under the Family Code. A California case involved a husband's daily written rules. Advocates warn that anti-abuse laws can be misused against victims, as in the Tamika Malayley case in Australia. The hosts note prevention ideas and women's equality.

segments.title: Progress on domestic violence and hotline information
segments.summary: The hosts cite Violence Against Women Act outcomes and note that data on coercive control is lacking. They give the National Domestic Violence Hotline information and encourage seeking help.

segments.title: Listener mail: The World Before Your Feet
segments.summary: A listener recommends the documentary The World Before Your Feet about Matt Green's walk of every New York City street.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank the listener and invite documentary recommendations.
